strengths: Novel and relevant problem formulation: While existing backdoor attacks against VLMs typically focus on static triggers or classification/text generation tasks, this paper is among the first to systematically investigate multi-target, input-aware backdoor attacks against VLM-based visual grounding systems.

Well-designed technical approach: Conditioning an input-aware U-Net generator on the textual embedding of arbitrary target objects, jointly optimized with perceptual regularization (L1 + LPIPS) and the language modeling loss, effectively balances trigger stealthiness and controllability across open-vocabulary grounding targets.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The authors evaluate across three modern open-source VLMs (LLaVA-1.5, InternVL-2.5, Ferret) on multiple grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO/+/g, Flickr30k Entities, ShowUI), comparing against several adapted input-aware baselines and testing resilience against various detection and sanitization defenses.

Comprehensive qualitative and supplementary evaluations: The paper provides informative ablations, defense tests, real-world case studies on photographs and GUI screenshots, and transferability assessments across datasets and tasks.
weaknesses: Threat model practicality at test time: Because the trigger generator $G_\phi$ requires both the target text $z_o$ and the exact input image $x$ to synthesize the perturbation $r$, the attacker must actively intercept or craft the specific image before it is processed by the model. This makes the operational threat model closer to an adversarial perturbation than a standard passive backdoor trigger (e.g., a physical artifact or fixed watermarking patch). A clearer discussion of realistic threat deployment channels would strengthen the submission.

Relatively modest Attack Success Rates (ASR): Across most datasets, the ASR@0.5 ranges between 35% and 68% (and drops to 25–35% on ShowUI). While the authors reasonably attribute this to the open-vocabulary nature and diversity of unseen candidate objects, the reliability of the attack remains limited compared to classic backdoor standards.

Heuristic nature of the theoretical analysis: Proposition 1 largely relies on standard first-order Taylor expansion and local smoothness assumptions (A1–A3) adapted from adversarial perturbation literature, offering limited new technical insights beyond formalizing the intuition that text-conditioned cross-attention alignment amplifies target gradient components.

strengths: Timely and novel problem formulation: The paper formalizes the first multi-target, input-aware backdoor attack against VLM-based visual grounding, moving beyond traditional static-trigger/fixed-target setups to tackle an open-vocabulary downstream task critical for embodied AI and GUI agents.

Sound and effective methodology: The proposed IAG leverages a text-conditioned U-Net to inject semantic information of arbitrary target objects into the visual input, optimized jointly with the VLM via language modeling and perceptual reconstruction objectives ($L_1$ and LPIPS).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors conduct extensive experiments across three representative VLMs (LLaVA-v1.5, InternVL-2.5, Ferret) on multiple grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, Flickr30k Entities, and ShowUI). IAG consistently outperforms adapted baselines while maintaining clean accuracy (less than 3% drop).

Thorough validation of stealthiness and defense robustness: The submission includes detailed imperceptibility metrics (PSNR, L1, LPIPS), tests against existing detection-based (Spectral Signature, Beatrix) and adaptive defenses (filtering, JPEG, quantization, PAR), transferability tests, and latency profiling.
weaknesses: Practicality and clarity of the inference threat model: While publishing poisoned model weights on platforms like HuggingFace is a realistic distribution vector, at inference time the attacker must dynamically perturb the user's input image using the generator $G_\phi$ conditioned on an attacker-specified target object. The paper would benefit from a more concrete discussion of how the attacker intercepts and modifies image feeds in practical deployment settings (e.g., web-based GUI agents vs. embodied camera inputs).

Modest performance margin over adapted baselines in certain benchmarks: While IAG demonstrates large gains on Flickr30k and ShowUI, its performance margin over Imperio is relatively narrow in several referring expression settings (e.g., Table 1 on RefCOCO: 58.9% vs. 55.2% on LLaVA, and 66.9% vs. 65.5% on InternVL). A more detailed analysis explaining when and why the text-conditioned U-Net provides substantial advantages over MLP/autoencoder architectures would strengthen the paper.

Moderate absolute attack success rate (ASR): The overall ASR ranges between 25% and 68%, falling considerably short of typical backdoor attack rates (>90%) seen in classification or static VLM backdoors. Although the open-vocabulary nature and unseen candidate objects partially explain this, it also reflects practical limitations in attack reliability.

Heuristic nature of the theoretical analysis: The theoretical justification in Section 3.6 and Appendix B relies heavily on Assumption A3 (target-aligned feature shift with high probability), which essentially assumes that the trigger effectively aligns with the margin gradient—the very property one would hope to establish.

strengths: Explores a novel and relevant security problem: extending backdoor attacks to open-vocabulary, generative visual grounding in vision-language models (VLMs) under a dynamic, multi-target setting.

The proposed method employs a text-conditioned U-Net generator with cross-modal attention to synthesize image-adaptive, target-conditioned perturbations, trained jointly with the VLM using both language modeling and perceptual losses (L1 + LPIPS).

Extensive experimental evaluation across three modern VLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, InternVL-2.5, Ferret) and five diverse visual grounding / GUI grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, Flickr30k Entities, ShowUI).

Thorough evaluation of defense mechanisms, including both representation-based detection methods (Spectral Signature, Beatrix) and image/model sanitization techniques (filtering, JPEG compression, quantization, PAR), showing strong resilience.
Comprehensive supplementary analyses, including ablation studies, perceptual fidelity metrics (PSNR, LPIPS), cross-dataset transferability, and qualitative case studies on GUI and real-world scenes.
weaknesses: Threat model practicality: At inference time, the attack requires generating an image-specific perturbation via an auxiliary text-conditioned neural network conditioned on both the input image and the target text. This blurs the line between backdoor attacks (which typically trigger autonomously upon encountering a fixed or semantic cue in the wild) and dynamic test-time adversarial attacks, limiting the realism in typical poisoning/backdoor scenarios.

Moderate Attack Success Rates (ASR): The achieved ASR@0.5 remains relatively low in several complex settings (e.g., 25.7%–34.7% on ShowUI, ~40%–53% on Flickr30k and RefCOCOg). While open-vocabulary grounding with numerous candidate targets is inherently challenging, an attack failing 45%–75% of the time raises questions regarding operational reliability.

Theoretical analysis relies on circular assumptions: Proposition 1 assumes in Assumption A3 that the cosine similarity between the margin gradient and the trigger-induced feature shift is already lower-bounded by gamma > 0 with high probability. This essentially assumes the attack direction is already aligned, reducing the proposition to a basic first-order Taylor expansion bound rather than explaining how or why the generator achieves this alignment.

Baseline comparisons: For several benchmarks (e.g., RefCOCOg with InternVL-2.5), earlier classification-adapted baselines such as Imperio achieve performance very close to IAG (e.g., 52.4% vs. 50.2% ASR), warranting deeper analysis into the architectural trade-offs between the U-Net generator and simpler conditional mappers.

strengths: Timely and relevant focus: Grounding-capable VLMs are foundational for embodied AI, GUI agents, and robotic navigation. Exploring vulnerability and backdoor risks specifically in generative visual grounding is important and underexplored compared to traditional classification tasks.

Input-aware semantic trigger design: Utilizing a text-conditional U-Net conditioned on the desired target object description enables dynamic, open-vocabulary backdoor triggering that overrides arbitrary user queries.

Solid empirical evaluation across multiple architectures: The method is validated across multiple representative open-source VLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, and Ferret-7B) on several standard benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-2017), showing high ASR@0.5 with minimal degradation on benign tasks.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablation studies (verifying joint training, reconstruction loss, and language loss), evaluations against standard backdoor defenses (Spectral Signature, Beatrix, PAR), poison rate sensitivity, and cross-dataset transferability.
weaknesses: Threat model practicality concerns: The attack requires training/fine-tuning the victim model (a supply-chain poisoning assumption) and, at inference time, intercepting the input image to run a forward pass through the conditioned U-Net generator. If an adversary has man-in-the-middle capability to intercept and modify the input image stream at inference time, the realistic threat setting needs clearer justification compared to simply altering the image directly or hijacking prompt queries.

Overstated theoretical analysis: Section 5 and Appendix A present 'proofs' of existence and convergence. However, the theoretical derivations rely on overly simplistic assumptions (e.g., constructing an artificial gated two-branch model $F_{\phi^*} = (1-p(I))LM_{clean} + p(I)B_t$, assuming the model inherently obeys a binary trigger gate, and assuming linear/NTK PL convergence conditions that do not faithfully model generative autoregressive decoder dynamics). Framing these heuristics as formal theoretical guarantees is an overstatement.

Lack of standard quantitative stealthiness/image quality metrics: Stealthiness is argued primarily through visual examples in Figure 3 and the use of the smooth $L_1$ loss. The paper lacks standard quantitative perceptual distortion metrics, such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, across the evaluation benchmarks to objectively verify that triggers are imperceptible.

Noticeable drafting and formatting errors: There are several glaring formatting issues throughout the manuscript. Multiple equations are incorrectly numbered as '(0)' (pages 3) and '(-2)' (pages 4, 5, 10). Furthermore, Table 8 on page 12 has an unfilled placeholder caption ('Table 8: Caption').

strengths: The paper targets an under-explored and practically relevant threat: backdoor vulnerabilities in vision-language models (VLMs) tailored for visual grounding tasks.
Formulating the attack to handle open-vocabulary, input-aware target objects using a text-conditional U-Net is a sensible design that overcomes the limitation of fixed-target static triggers.

The empirical evaluation is conducted across multiple modern open-source VLMs (InternVL-2.5-8B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, Ferret-7B) and standard grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, COCO), supplemented by ablation studies and tests against several backdoor defenses.
weaknesses: Threat model and attack practical plausibility: The proposed method requires an attacker to actively intercept each input image at inference time and run a deep text-conditional U-Net conditioned on the target description before passing the image to the victim VLM. Because the perturbation is dynamically generated per-image and per-target at test time, the distinction from input-specific adversarial attacks/perturbations becomes blurred, weakening the standard motivation of backdoor attacks (where simple, static triggers or lightweight visual marks are planted to trigger pre-conditioned behaviors).

Flawed and superficial theoretical analysis: Propositions 1 and 2 provide little substantive insight. Proposition 1 relies on standard universal approximation hand-waving (assuming ViT and U-Net have universal approximation capacity and positing an idealized two-branch binary gating function). Proposition 2 asserts convergence by assuming the loss satisfies the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, which does not hold globally for deep multimodal architectures trained via LoRA. These sections appear decorative rather than mathematically rigorous.

Weak and unconvincing baseline comparisons: The baselines compared in Table 2 (BadEncoder and TrojVLM) were designed for pre-training encoder embeddings or fixed-target multimodal classification/VQA with static triggers. Forcing them into a multi-target grounding task naturally causes them to fail (~0-13% ASR). Stronger and more relevant input-aware backdoor baselines (e.g., dynamic generator-based backdoor attacks adapted to image-to-image or conditional generation) should be evaluated.

Severe formatting and presentation flaws: Equation numbering throughout the manuscript is broken, displaying negative equation numbers (e.g., Eq. (-2) on pages 3, 4, 5, and 10) and repeated zeros (e.g., Eq. (0) on page 3). This indicates inadequate proofreading and layout preparation.

Discrepancies in reported results: In Table 1, InternVL-2.5-8B achieves an ASR@0.5 of 65.9% on RefCOCO (val), while Table 2 reports an ASR@0.5 of 82.4% on RefCOCO. While Table 2 uses a 100-target subset, the textual explanation in Section 6.2 fails to clearly contextualize why performance on this restricted subset is drastically higher than the main benchmark results.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting and timely security topic: backdoor vulnerabilities in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) tailored for visual grounding, which is relevant for embodied AI and GUI agent safety.

The proposed approach formulates an input-aware and text-conditional trigger generator using a conditional U-Net, attempting to handle the open-vocabulary nature of visual grounding tasks rather than relying on static triggers.

The empirical evaluation spans three different VLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, and Ferret-7B) across multiple grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, and COCO-2017), including evaluations against several defense methods.
weaknesses: The threat model presents practical and conceptual limitations. The attacker is assumed to control both the model training phase (to embed the backdoor) and the inference pipeline (to inject input-adaptive triggers generated by the conditional U-Net into the input image). If an adversary already has the capability to actively manipulate input images at test time, the motivation for concurrently backdooring the model weights is weakened, as adversarial perturbations or prompt injection could potentially achieve similar disruption without supply-chain poisoning.

The theoretical analysis in Section 5 and Appendix A does not provide substantive guarantees. The existence proof (Proposition 1) relies entirely on classical universal approximation properties and an idealized gating mechanism, which trivially holds for arbitrary functions without explaining the interaction between cross-modal attention, LoRA fine-tuning, and grounding regression. Similarly, the convergence claims (Proposition 2, Lemmas 1–4) assert smoothness and Polyak-Łojasiewicz conditions under strong assumptions (e.g., linear/NTK-linearized classifiers on separable data) that do not translate to the non-convex joint optimization of a conditional U-Net and a 7B/8B VLM.

The baseline comparisons in Table 2 are not well matched to the task. BadEncoder and TrojVLM were developed for representation learning and classification/captioning settings with fixed targets; forcing them into a heuristic 100-class setup does not constitute a strong or natural baseline. The paper would benefit from comparisons against test-time adversarial attacks on visual grounding or other dynamic trigger generation schemes.

The overall attack success rate (ASR@0.5) is relatively moderate (typically 40%–66% across benchmarks, and below 50% on Ferret-7B and COCO-2017). Given that the adversary trains the network and modifies the test image, a failure rate of 35%–60% indicates that the trigger often fails to reliably force the model to ground the attacker's designated target.

The manuscript contains several formatting and presentation flaws. Multiple equations in Section 3, Section 4, Section 5, and Appendix A are mislabeled with broken equation numbers such as '(0)' and '(-2)'. Additionally, technical details regarding the U-Net architecture (e.g., whether it is fine-tuned from a pretrained latent diffusion model or trained from scratch) and text encoder specifications are insufficiently detailed in the main methodology.
